newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan giants applaud WTO infotech progress.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan giants applaud WTO infotech progress.

text.p: Taiwan's prodigious computer exporters on Friday hailed the World Trade Organisation's progress towards freeing commerce in information technology, saying it would benefit the global industry.

Acer Inc and First International Computer shrugged off concerns that a pact signed by 28 states -- including Taiwan -- to eliminate tariffs by 2000 would lead to a "technology invasion" of less-developed countries.
"Many countries are afraid of the so-called technology invasion and therefore are against lowering tariffs," Acer chairman Stan Shih said in a statement.

"But this merely hinders full implementation and development of technology," Shih said. "The main reason Taiwan's high-tech industry is among the world leaders is because the government already gives very little protection to the industry."
Taiwan boasts one of the world's largest information technology industries, with computer production value totalling US$21.3 billion in 1995.
U.S. officials at a WTO meeting in Singapore said the 28 countries that signed the pact represented 84 percent of global trade in information technology products.
Another six countries had committed to the pact, bringing the global trade covered by the deal to over 90 percent.
Inclusion of 90 percent of trade was the key hurdle set by the European Union and United States for implementation of the information technology agreement.
First International, second only to Acer among Taiwan computer makers, said the agreement would boost exports of the island's information technology.

"The fewer restrictions there are, the more companies will be willing to consider overseas investments to diversify operations, especially the bigger companies," said Rick Lee, First International spokesman.

Lee said while less-developed countries initially may lose out to stronger, market-tested foreign competitors, they also would be forced eventually to raise their standards to meet the global challenge.
"There's going to be a transition period for some industries," Lee said. "But competition eventually will improve all industries and that is the ultimate benefit of free trade."
The WTO estimates world exports of information technology products totalled around $600 billion in 1995. Analysts say the sector is growing at least 15 percent annually.
